note.text:
The percentage by mass of an element in a compound is:
(mass of that element in one formula unit ÷ relative formula mass) × 100 per cent.
Steps: work out the relative formula mass; multiply the relative atomic mass of the element by how many atoms of it there are; divide and multiply by 100.
Example: water, H2O, Mr = 18. Hydrogen: 2 × 1 = 2, so 2/18 × 100 = 11.1 per cent. Oxygen: 16/18 × 100 = 88.9 per cent. The percentages add up to 100.
The same idea tells a farmer which fertiliser carries the most nitrogen per bag, and tells a miner how much metal an ore holds.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to work out the percentage by mass of any element in a compound, and use it to compare fertilisers or ores.
Builds on: Lesson {19} (relative formula mass) and Lesson {21} (mole calculations).
Leads to: Lesson {24}, which runs this calculation backwards to find a formula from percentages.

sections.heading: The calculation
sections.text:
Percentage by mass of an element = (mass of that element in one formula unit ÷ relative formula mass) × {100}.
Water, {formula('H2O')}, Mr = {18}:
• hydrogen: {2} × {1} = {2}, so {2} ÷ {18} × {100} = {11.1} per cent;
• oxygen: {16} ÷ {18} × {100} = {88.9} per cent.
The two add up to {100}, which is a useful check.
Count EVERY atom of the element. In {formula('H2SO4')} (Mr = {98}) the oxygen is {4} × {16} = {64}, so {64} ÷ {98} × {100} = {65.3} per cent.

mistake.wrong: the percentage of oxygen in {formula('H2SO4')} is {16} ÷ {98} × {100}
mistake.why: There are {4} oxygen atoms in the formula, so their total mass is {64}.

worked_example.problem: Find the percentage by mass of {E} in {formula(F)}.
steps: There {atomCount(F, E) == 1 ? 'is' : 'are'} {atomCount(F, E)} atom of {E}, of mass {atomCount(F, E) * ram(E)}.

cards.idea: Percentage = (mass of the element ÷ relative formula mass) × {100}.
Count every atom of the element in the formula.
The percentages of all the elements add up to {100}.

pick.q: The percentages by mass of all the elements in a compound are added. What should the total be?
w: It depends on the compound
More than {100} per cent for a large molecule
Less than {100} per cent
e: The whole is always the sum of its parts, whatever the compound.
The parts cannot add to more than the whole.
Nothing is left out: every atom belongs to one of the elements.
pick.y: Every atom belongs to one element, so the masses add up to the whole formula mass.

pick.q: A pupil finds that a compound is {40} per cent carbon and {70} per cent oxygen. What does this show?
pick.r: A mistake has been made, because the total is more than {100} per cent
w: The compound holds another element as well
The compound is a mixture
Nothing is wrong
e: Another element would make the total even larger, not smaller.
Even a mixture's percentages must add to {100}.
A total above {100} per cent is impossible.
pick.y: The percentages of the parts can never add to more than the whole.

pick.q: Which fertiliser carries the most nitrogen for each kilogram bought?
pick.r: Urea, {formula('CO(NH2)2')}, at about {47} per cent nitrogen
w: Ammonium sulphate, at about {21} per cent
Ammonium nitrate, at about {35} per cent
Sodium nitrate, at about {16} per cent
e: Ammonium sulphate carries a heavy sulphate group, so its nitrogen percentage is low.
Ammonium nitrate is good, but urea is better still.
Sodium nitrate carries a heavy sodium atom for each nitrogen.
pick.y: The smaller the rest of the formula, the larger the share of the mass that is nitrogen.

pick.q: Why does a mining company care about the percentage of metal in an ore?
pick.r: It tells them how much metal each tonne of rock will give, and so whether mining is worth the cost
w: It tells them how deep the ore lies
It tells them the colour of the metal
It tells them how hard the rock is
e: Depth is found by surveying, not from the formula.
The colour has nothing to do with the percentage by mass.
Hardness is a physical property of the rock.
pick.y: Haematite, {formula('Fe2O3')}, is {70} per cent iron, so {100} tonnes of pure ore would give {70} tonnes of iron.

questions.prompt: Find the percentage by mass of {E} in {formula(F)}. Give your answer to {1} decimal place.

misconceptions.explain: Divide the mass of the ELEMENT by the whole formula mass.
Count every atom of {E}: there are {atomCount(F, E)}.

questions.prompt: What is the total mass of {E} in one formula unit of {formula(F)}?

misconceptions.explain: There are {atomCount(F, E)} atoms of {E}, not one.
{molarMass(F)} is the mass of the WHOLE formula unit.

questions.prompt: What mass of {E}, in grams, is there in {m} g of {formula(F)}? Give your answer to {1} decimal place.

misconceptions.explain: That is the PERCENTAGE; apply it to the {m} g given.
Only part of the {m} g is {E}.

solution: {E} is {roundTo(percentMass(F, E), 0.1)} per cent of {formula(F)} by mass.
{roundTo(percentMass(F, E), 0.1)} per cent of {m} g = {answer} g.
